column3: Agrippa said to Paul, “You are permitted to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and began making his defense:
“Concerning all the things of which I am accused by Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate that I am about to make my defense before you today,
especially because you are an expert in all the customs and disputes among Jews. Therefore I ask you to listen to me patiently.
“My way of life from my youth, which from the beginning was among my nation and in Jerusalem, all the Jews know.
They have known me from the beginning, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest sect of our religion I lived as a Pharisee.
And now I stand being judged for hope in the promise made by God to our fathers,
to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, earnestly serving night and day. Concerning this hope I am accused by Jews, O king.
Why is it judged unbelievable among you if God raises the dead?
“I myself indeed thought it necessary to do many things against the name of Jesus the Nazarene.
And this is what I did in Jerusalem. I shut up many of the holy ones in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were being put to death, I cast my vote against them.
And throughout all the synagogues, often punishing them, I tried to force them to blaspheme. And being exceedingly enraged against them, I persecuted them even as far as foreign cities.
“In this activity, while traveling to Damascus with authority and commission from the chief priests,
at midday, O king, along the road I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those traveling with me.
And when we all had fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’
I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

But get up and stand on your feet, for I appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you as a servant and witness both of the things in which you have seen me and of the things in which I will appear to you,
rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you,
to open their eyes, to turn them from darkness to light and from the authority of Satan to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in me.’
“Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,
but first to those in Damascus and Jerusalem, and throughout all the region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, I was declaring that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.
Because of these things the Jews seized me in the temple and were trying to kill me.
Therefore, having obtained help from God, I stand to this day testifying to both small and great, saying nothing beyond the things the prophets and Moses said were going to happen:
that the Christ was to suffer and, being first from resurrection of the dead, was to proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.”
Now as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “You are out of your mind, Paul! Great learning is driving you to madness.”
But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I speak words of truth and sound judgment.
For the king knows about these things, to whom I also speak boldly, because I am persuaded that none of these things escapes his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time you are persuading me to become a Christian!”
Paul said, “I would pray to God that whether in a short or long time, not only you but also all those hearing me today might become such as I am, except for these chains.”
Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those sitting with them,
and withdrawing, they began speaking to one another, saying, “This man is doing nothing worthy of death or chains.”
And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
